title: Steve Eisman’s Masterclass on Financial Literacy | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 24
summary: Eisman teaches long-term investing, thesis discipline, short-selling risk, valuation methods, sector behavior and interest-rate transmission. He favors simple US equity-index portfolios, insists on explicit thesis tests, and explains why short exposures grow when prices rise. His sector-based approach is practical, but several definitions and historical explanations need correction, including enterprise value, REIT cash-flow measures, the 2025 drawdown arithmetic and the claim that the Fed controls only one rate.
assessment: The most reusable contribution is the distinction between an investment thesis and the emotional reasons for continuing to hold it. Basic short-sale and discounting mathematics are sound when their assumptions are stated. Portfolio preferences are not universal suitability findings, and sector conventions are not valuation laws. The valuation primer contains material technical mistakes, so its formulas should be checked before reuse.
framework_points: Write the investment thesis and the observable facts that would disprove it before becoming attached to the stock.
Distinguish business deterioration, valuation and the funding constraints that can force a short seller to cover.
Learn the metrics used by sector specialists, but reconcile them to cash generation and the balance sheet.
Separate a defensive business from a stock guaranteed to avoid losses.
He distrusts decades-long DCF precision and prefers nearer-term business fundamentals.
tools_and_charts: Forward P/E and dated consensus estimates.
Enterprise value / EBITDA, price / tangible book, DCF and REIT FFO/AFFO.
Position weights, borrow costs, short interest and short-squeeze mechanics.
Sector weights and relative returns during the February-May 2025 selloff and rebound.
Yield curve, net interest margin and discount-rate sensitivity.
transcript_cautions: Read all 1,502 caption segments through the closing disclosure.
Many examples explicitly use June 18, 2025 prices and consensus estimates despite the September 8 listing date; they are not September spot valuations.
Captions corrupt EBITDA, AFFO, company names and some numbers. The drawdown correction uses the stated index levels, so it does not depend on an assumed transcription of an unviewed table.
The sector-weight discussion gives inconsistent rounded weights in different passages; the displayed tables were not independently inspected.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman presents; speaker attribution follows the full dialogue.

claims.claim: Excess leverage and mortgage exposure made the pre-2008 financial system fragile.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare leverage, funding and mortgage exposures before the crisis.
claims.reason: The FCIC documents leverage, fragile funding and mortgage-linked losses. This is a retrospective explanation, not a new forecast win.

evidence.title: Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13
evidence.finding: Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

claims.claim: A short initially equal to 4% of the portfolio becomes an 8% position when its stock doubles.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.reason: Gross short liability doubles, but the equity denominator also falls from the loss unless other gains offset it. With no offset, exposure becomes about 8.33%.
claims.next_check: Separate gross liability from net portfolio equity.

proof.derivation: Start with equity 100 and short liability 4. A doubling creates liability 8 and loss 4, leaving equity 96; 8 / 96 = 8.33%. The stated 8% requires equity to stay 100.

claims.claim: An unhedged short has theoretically unlimited loss, and rising exposure can force risk managers to cover.

claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: For fixed shares N, short profit before costs is N × (sale price - repurchase price); there is no fixed upper bound on the latter.

evidence.title: Financial ratios and measures: enterprise value
evidence.finding: Operating enterprise value nets cash from equity plus debt and adds minority interests where appropriate; debt plus equity alone includes non-operating cash.

claims.claim: EBITDA adds interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization back to net earnings.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: EBITDA = net income + interest expense + tax expense + depreciation + amortization, with consistent scope.

claims.claim: EBITDA per share is always greater than EPS.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect signs and definitions rather than assume every add-back is positive.
claims.reason: Usually positive add-backs make it larger, but the word always fails when net interest or tax benefits outweigh depreciation and other additions.
claims.next_check: Inspect signs and definitions rather than assume every add-back is positive.

proof.derivation: If net income is 100, tax expense is -30 and total remaining add-backs are 10, EBITDA is 80, below net income. Dividing both by the same share count preserves the inequality.

claims.claim: John Malone pioneered EBITDA to show the cash-generating potential of debt-funded telecom expansion.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check contemporary Malone statements and reconcile cash flow, capex and borrowing.
claims.reason: The origin and personal rationale are historical assertions without an inspected contemporaneous source here. EBITDA is not itself cash available after investment.

claims.claim: EBITDA can give a misleading economic picture by excluding the cost of maintaining capital-intensive assets.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The limitation follows from the metric. This supports a measurement warning, not a verdict on every company valued using EBITDA.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Adding depreciation back and omitting capital expenditure leaves replacement investment outside EBITDA; identical EBITDA can coexist with very different free cash flow.

claims.claim: Book value per share uses common equity per share; tangible book removes goodwill and other intangibles.

claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Tangible common equity per share = (common equity - goodwill - other applicable intangibles) / common shares.

claims.claim: REIT FFO is a cash-flow measure calculated from pretax earnings, adding depreciation and subtracting property gains and interest income.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman

claims.reason: The stated bridge conflates FFO with other measures. Nareit FFO begins with GAAP net income, and is expressly not GAAP operating cash flow; interest income is not a universal FFO subtraction.

evidence.title: 2025 supplemental definitions: FFO and FAD
evidence.finding: Nareit FFO starts with GAAP net income, adjusts real-estate depreciation and sale gains/losses, and is not GAAP operating cash flow. The FAD reconciliation deducts recurring capital and leasing costs.

claims.next_check: Use the issuer’s reconciliation to the Nareit definition and distinguish cash-flow statements.

claims.claim: AFFO adds back capital expenditures and then deducts maintenance capex as a standard REIT valuation formula.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect the individual issuer’s AFFO bridge and avoid double-counting capex.
claims.reason: AFFO is not standardized. Recurring capex is commonly deducted from FFO-based measures; capital spending is not generally an expense already removed from FFO that can simply be added back.

evidence.title: Q2 2026 definitions: AFFO
evidence.finding: AFFO deducts recurring capital expenditures and leasing costs from adjusted FFO. Nareit has not standardized AFFO, so company definitions differ.

claims.next_check: Inspect the individual issuer’s AFFO bridge and avoid double-counting capex.

claims.reason: This is the correct distinction between relative defensiveness and absolute capital protection; the specific sample returns remain separately unresolved.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Healthcare missed the rally because Trump made Medicare and Medicaid pay the lowest foreign drug price.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Distinguish announcement, binding implementation, affected products and event-study evidence.
claims.reason: A most-favored-nation initiative was announced, but the order directs targets and possible later rulemaking rather than an immediate universal price substitution. It also does not establish the entire sector’s causal return attribution.

evidence.title: Most-favored-nation drug-pricing executive order
evidence.finding: The order directs price targets and possible later rulemaking if progress is inadequate. It does not instantly replace every Medicare and Medicaid drug price with the lowest foreign price.

claims.next_check: Distinguish announcement, binding implementation, affected products and event-study evidence.

claims.claim: June sector weights show technology dominates the US index and explain why a tech bull should prefer US equities to Europe.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconstruct the same-date weights and compare broad economic exposures under consistent definitions.
claims.reason: The stated weights are not fully consistent across later passages, and the investment conclusion needs valuation and overlap analysis as well as sector share.
claims.next_check: Reconstruct the same-date weights and compare broad economic exposures under consistent definitions.

claims.claim: Within sectors, payments and biotech can be growth businesses while traditional banks are cyclical and staples are relatively defensive.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: The useful lesson is to classify by economics rather than the sector label alone. These are broad conventions with many exceptions, not forecasts for every constituent.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Cord cutting and streaming have damaged the former defensive character of traditional media and cable.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate linear-video decline from broadband, connectivity and other segment economics.
claims.reason: The mechanism is plausible, but company-specific cash flow, subscriber trends and valuations determine how much value is impaired.
claims.next_check: Separate linear-video decline from broadband, connectivity and other segment economics.

claims.claim: Celebrity brands and influencers have intensified beauty competition and hurt established companies.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare brand shares, marketing costs and incumbent margins over the specified period.
claims.reason: The industry-change thesis lacks a matched market-share and profit attribution study here.
claims.next_check: Compare brand shares, marketing costs and incumbent margins over the specified period.

claims.claim: Solar is the principal growth exception within the S&P Energy sector.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use official GICS categories when explaining S&P sector weights.
claims.reason: The discussion confuses an energy-related economic activity with index classification. GICS places solar-module and cell manufacturers in Information Technology, with renewable electricity elsewhere.

evidence.title: GICS methodology, Information Technology definitions
evidence.finding: The Information Technology semiconductor category includes manufacturers of solar modules and cells. Solar is not simply a subsector of the GICS Energy sector.

claims.next_check: Use official GICS categories when explaining S&P sector weights.

claims.claim: Higher financing costs and adverse federal policy weakened residential solar demand and stocks.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare financed monthly payments, installations and company-specific demand alongside policy changes.
claims.reason: The proposed channels are plausible, but this passage does not isolate them from pricing, inventories, state policy or company execution. The $30,000 system price is illustrative.
claims.next_check: Compare financed monthly payments, installations and company-specific demand alongside policy changes.

claims.claim: Office REITs lost their former defensive character as office-property values declined.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect vacancies, leases, valuations, debt maturities and actual asset sales.
claims.reason: The broad diagnosis needs dated, property-specific evidence; it does not establish that the downturn is over or that every REIT has the same exposure.
claims.next_check: Inspect vacancies, leases, valuations, debt maturities and actual asset sales.

claims.claim: Regulated utilities have relatively predictable profits and defensive characteristics.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect rate cases, capital plans, recovery mechanisms and financing needs.
claims.reason: Regulation can improve visibility, but allowed returns, cost recovery, debt financing and exceptional liabilities prevent guaranteed profitability.
claims.next_check: Inspect rate cases, capital plans, recovery mechanisms and financing needs.

claims.claim: The Fed controls only the federal funds rate and no other interest rate.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Distinguish administered rates, the funds target and the effective market rate.
claims.reason: It directly administers reserve-interest, reverse-repo and discount rates as well. The useful distinction is between policy instruments and market-determined longer-term yields, not that the Fed sets only one rate.

evidence.title: Ample-reserves monetary-policy implementation
evidence.finding: The Fed sets administered reserve-interest and reverse-repo rates to guide the federal funds market rate. The discount rate is also administered; long-term yields are not directly fixed by the funds target.

claims.next_check: Distinguish administered rates, the funds target and the effective market rate.

claims.claim: Long rates usually exceed short rates because lending for longer is riskier.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Decompose yields into expected policy rates and term premia.
claims.reason: A term premium can contribute, but expected future short rates and changing risk premia also determine the curve. No historical frequency or exclusive causal decomposition is established.
claims.next_check: Decompose yields into expected policy rates and term premia.

claims.claim: For fixed promised bond cash flows, a higher price implies a lower yield.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The inverse relationship is correct when cash flows and maturity are held constant.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: Bond price is the sum of fixed positive cash flows discounted at yield; increasing yield reduces each present value.

claims.claim: Fear of recession can pull long yields below short yields, but inversion does not perfectly predict recession.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Compare a defined spread and lead window with an official recession chronology.
claims.reason: This is a qualified interpretation rather than a deterministic signal. The passage supplies no specified spread, lead time or false-positive study.
claims.next_check: Compare a defined spread and lead window with an official recession chronology.

claims.claim: A steeper yield curve increases bank net interest margins because banks fund short and lend long.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Model asset and liability repricing rather than use slope alone.
claims.reason: The stylized maturity transformation is useful, but the implication is not automatic: deposit betas, asset repricing, hedges, funding mix and credit losses can offset it.
claims.next_check: Model asset and liability repricing rather than use slope alone.

proof.derivation: Suppose the market short rate is unchanged and the long rate rises 1 point, steepening the curve. If a bank raises previously low deposit rates by 2 points to retain funding while asset yield rises 1 point, its spread falls 1 point. The claimed result requires assumptions about deposit pricing and asset repricing.

claims.claim: Rising long-term rates need not hurt stocks when they reflect stronger growth without excessive inflation.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.
claims.reason: He qualifies the usual inverse-rate heuristic. The net outcome depends on earnings revisions and discount rates, so this is a scenario framework.
claims.next_check: Use as a decision rule, not a dated return forecast.

claims.claim: Inflation-driven Fed tightening caused the 2022 equity decline, although the feared recession did not occur.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Separate price and total returns, realized recession dates and the contribution of earnings versus discount rates.
claims.reason: The rate and earnings-risk channels are plausible, but the attribution is not isolated. The cited roughly 18% decline requires a total-return rather than price-only definition.
claims.next_check: Separate price and total returns, realized recession dates and the contribution of earnings versus discount rates.

claims.claim: With projected positive cash flows fixed, increasing the discount rate reduces DCF value.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: This is correct conditional mathematics. Actual market moves also change growth forecasts and risk premia.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: For each positive future cash flow C at time t, C/(1+r)^t declines as r rises; summing preserves the direction.

claims.claim: Cash flows concentrated farther in the future are more sensitive to discount-rate changes than equally valued nearer cash flows.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.
claims.reason: The duration mechanism is correct; it does not guarantee that every growth stock underperforms every staple whenever rates rise.
claims.next_check: Check the stated assumptions and calculation.

proof.derivation: The proportional sensitivity of a single discounted cash flow is -t/(1+r); later t means larger sensitivity at the same rate.
